content: Chickenpox, also known as varicella, is a highly contagious infectious disease caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It is primarily a childhood illness, with most children contracting and recovering from it. The disease is characterized by the development of hundreds of itchy, fluid-filled blisters that eventually burst and form crusts. The same virus is responsible for causing shingles (herpes zoster) in adults. Chickenpox does not show any racial or gender predisposition. Treatment is generally symptomatic, except in immunocompromised patients. The first description of chickenpox was provided by Razi, an Iranian physician. Giovanni Filippo elaborated on it in the mid-1500s, and in 1767, William Heberden distinguished chickenpox from smallpox. The live attenuated vaccine for chickenpox was introduced in 1974. Chickenpox is transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized droplets from nasopharyngeal secretions or direct contact with vesicular fluid from an infected individual. The incubation period ranges from 10 to 21 days after exposure. The virus initially proliferates in the regional lymph nodes of the upper respiratory tract, leading to viremia. Viremia results in widespread viral invasion of capillary endothelial cells and the epidermis. Infection of the Malpighian layer of the skin causes intercellular and intracellular edema, leading to the formation of characteristic vesicles. The causative agent of chickenpox is the varicella-zoster virus, also known as human herpesvirus 3 (HHV-3). Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets or contact with vesicular fluid from skin lesions. Differential diagnosis of chickenpox involves ruling out other rash-like conditions, except for smallpox, which is distinct. Chickenpox is endemic and primarily spreads through respiratory routes. Cases occur year-round but are more common in winter and early spring. In tropical regions, varicella infections are more prevalent among adults than children. Risk factors for contracting chickenpox include a lack of prior infection or vaccination, being a newborn (especially premature infants or those born to mothers without prior chickenpox infection), immunocompromised individuals, cancer patients, and those on immunosuppressant drugs. Routine screening for chickenpox is not recommended for the general population, as most adults have either been vaccinated or infected during childhood. However, screening is advised for specific groups, such as healthcare workers, pregnant women, newborns, HIV/AIDS patients, and individuals undergoing organ transplantation. If untreated, repeated scratching of chickenpox sores can lead to bacterial skin infections like cellulitis. In some cases, the infection can spread to the lungs, causing pneumonia, which can be fatal. While chickenpox is usually mild, serious complications such as bacterial skin infections in children and pneumonia in adults can occur. Pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk of severe complications. Pregnant women exposed to chickenpox may require urgent treatment to prevent complications for the baby, particularly before 20 weeks of gestation. The diagnosis of chickenpox is primarily clinical, based on the characteristic rash and associated symptoms. The rash typically begins on the head and trunk before spreading to the rest of the body. Symptoms include low-grade fever, intense itching, headache, malaise, anorexia, cough, and coryza. Laboratory tests are not routinely used but may include examination of vesicle fluid (e.g., Tzanck smear or direct fluorescent antibody testing) or blood tests for acute immunologic response (IgM) or immunity (IgG). Prenatal diagnosis of fetal varicella infection can be performed using ultrasound or PCR testing of amniotic fluid, though the risks of amniocentesis may outweigh the benefits. Chest X-rays may reveal diffuse lung cloudiness in cases of varicella pneumonia, a rare complication in children but more common in adults. CT scans and MRI have minimal diagnostic value unless complications arise. Ultrasound findings are not associated with chickenpox. Treatment for chickenpox in otherwise healthy individuals is usually symptomatic, focusing on relieving discomfort. Calamine lotion and colloidal oatmeal baths can help alleviate itching, while keeping fingernails trimmed short can prevent secondary skin infections caused by scratching. Vaccination is the primary preventive measure, with two doses recommended for children and unvaccinated adults. The first dose is given between 12-15 months of age, and the second dose is administered at 4-6 years of age, with a minimum interval of three months between doses. For adults aged 13 years or older, two doses are recommended, with at least 28 days between doses.
